title: Does the European Accessibility Act require service providers to train staff?
description: What Directive (EU) 2019/882 says about staff training: recital 20, Article 13 duties, the June 28, 2025 start date, service scope, and Portugal's law.
shortAnswer: The European Accessibility Act, Directive (EU) 2019/882, has applied to covered consumer services since June 28, 2025. Its articles do not impose a standalone training duty, but recital 20 states that service providers "should also ensure proper and continuous training of their personnel" on using accessible products and services, covering information provision, advice and advertising. Article 13 requires procedures that keep services conforming, which is hard to evidence without trained staff.
keyTakeaways: Recital 20 is the only place the Directive asks service providers to train staff. It is a recital, so the binding hook is Article 13 and national transposing law.
The Act applies to services provided to consumers after June 28, 2025 (Article 2(2)), including consumer banking, e-commerce, electronic communications, e-books, and elements of passenger transport.

Microenterprises providing services, meaning fewer than 10 persons and turnover or balance sheet of EUR 2 million or less, are exempt from the service accessibility requirements (Article 4(5) and Article 3(23)).
Article 14(5) makes service providers that claim a disproportionate burden renew that assessment at least every five years, and Annex VI counts training costs in the assessment.
Portugal transposed the Directive through Decreto-Lei n.º 82/2022 of December 6, 2022, with Portaria n.º 220/2023 setting technical requirements.
regulator: National market surveillance authorities and authorities responsible for checking compliance of services, designated by each Member State
appliesTo: Providers of electronic communications services and services giving access to audiovisual media services
Consumer banking service providers and e-commerce service providers
Providers of e-books and dedicated software
Air, bus, rail and waterborne passenger transport services for websites, apps, e-ticketing, travel information and self-service terminals
Manufacturers, importers and distributors of covered products such as consumer computers, payment terminals, ATMs, ticketing machines and e-readers

sections.heading: What does the Directive say about staff training?

blocks.text: The Directive mentions staff training for service providers once, in recital 20. It reads: "Service providers should also ensure proper and continuous training of their personnel in order to ensure that they are knowledgeable about how to use accessible products and services. That training should cover issues such as information provision, advice and advertising."

The same recital adds that subcontracting does not dilute the duty: where a service or part of it is subcontracted, "the accessibility of that service should not be compromised". Recitals explain the intent of the articles but do not create freestanding obligations. The training expectation therefore works through the operative duties in Article 13 and through whatever each Member State wrote into its transposing law.

blocks.title: Stated plainly
blocks.text: No article of Directive (EU) 2019/882 says "service providers shall train staff". Recital 20 says they should, and continuously. National law, contracts and regulator guidance may convert that expectation into a duty, so check the transposing act in each country of operation.

sections.heading: Which services are covered, and from when?

blocks.text: Article 2(2) applies the Directive to specified services provided to consumers after June 28, 2025. Article 31(1) required Member States to adopt and publish national measures by June 28, 2022, and Article 31(2) required them to apply those measures from June 28, 2025.

items: Electronic communications services, except transmission services used for machine-to-machine services.
Services providing access to audiovisual media services.

Elements of air, bus, rail and waterborne passenger transport: websites, mobile services, electronic tickets, transport information, and interactive self-service terminals in the Union (urban, suburban and regional transport is covered only for terminals).

blocks.text: Article 2(4) excludes some website and app content, including pre-recorded time-based media and office file formats published before June 28, 2025, third-party content the operator neither funds nor controls, and archives not updated after that date. Article 4(5) exempts microenterprises providing services from the Annex I service requirements. Article 3(23) defines a microenterprise as one that "employs fewer than 10 persons" with annual turnover or balance sheet total not exceeding EUR 2 million.

sections.heading: Which obligations make staff knowledge necessary?

blocks.text: Article 13 sets the service provider's duties, and most of them depend on people who know what accessible service delivery looks like. Under Article 13(1) providers must design and provide services in line with the accessibility requirements. Article 13(2) requires information under Annex V explaining how the service meets them, made available "in written and oral format, including in a manner which is accessible to persons with disabilities".

Article 13(3) requires "procedures are in place so that the provision of services remains in conformity", taking account of changes in the service, the requirements, and harmonized standards. Article 13(4) requires corrective action and immediate notification of the competent authority where a service does not conform. Article 13(5) requires cooperation with authorities on request.

Annex I, Section III, point (d) adds that support services, "help desks, call centres, technical support, relay services and training services", must where available provide information on the accessibility of the service and its compatibility with assistive technologies, in accessible modes of communication. Front line support staff are the people who deliver that requirement.

blocks.text: The same rows drop into a [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) by role. Teams that produce digital learning should also read the guide on [how to make e-learning accessible](/guides/how-to-make-elearning-accessible), because training content delivered to customers or staff through a covered service is itself part of what must be accessible.

sections.heading: How does training relate to the disproportionate burden test?

blocks.text: Training costs are one of the factors a provider must weigh if it claims that accessibility would impose a disproportionate burden. Article 14(1) limits the accessibility requirements where compliance would fundamentally alter a service or impose a disproportionate burden, and Article 14(2) requires an assessment using the Annex VI criteria.

Annex VI lists one-off organizational costs to include, among them "costs related to training human resources and acquiring competences on accessibility" and costs of developing guidance material. Article 14(3) requires the assessment to be documented and kept for five years after the service was last provided. Article 14(5) requires service providers to renew it when the service changes, when an authority asks, and "in any event, at least every five years". Article 14(6) bars providers that received outside funding for accessibility from relying on the burden exception at all.

sections.heading: What transitional periods apply, and how did Portugal transpose the Act?

blocks.text: Article 32 gives service providers some time for legacy products and contracts. Member States must provide a transitional period ending June 28, 2030 during which providers may keep using products lawfully used before that date, and service contracts agreed before June 28, 2025 may continue unaltered for up to five years. Self-service terminals in use before June 28, 2025 may stay in service until the end of their economically useful life, but no longer than 20 years.

As at November 2026, the [EUR-Lex national transposition page](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/NIM/?uri=CELEX:32019L0882) lists three Portuguese measures: Decreto-Lei n.º 82/2022 of December 6, 2022, which transposes the Directive; Declaração de Retificação n.º 5/2023 correcting it; and Declaração de Retificação n.º 17/2023 correcting Portaria n.º 220/2023 of July 20, 2023, which sets accessibility requirements and the criteria for assessing disproportionate burden. Organizations in Portugal should read those instruments alongside the existing pages on [Portugal's Labor Code continuous training duty](/regulations/portugal-labour-code-continuous-training) when budgeting training hours.

sections.heading: How should a covered provider structure accessibility training?

items: Confirm which services fall under Article 2(2) and whether the microenterprise exemption applies.
Identify roles by the article they deliver: builders (Annex I Section III(c)), communicators (Article 13(2)), support staff (Section III(d)), and owners of conformity procedures (Article 13(3)).
Give customer facing staff the recital 20 topics: how accessible features work, how to give accessible information and advice, and how to avoid inaccessible advertising.
Train digital teams on the harmonized standard or technical specification the service declares conformity with, and retrain when it changes.
Keep records per role and per standard version so the provider can respond to an Article 13(5) request.
Review the training whenever the service changes, which is also a trigger for an Article 14(5) reassessment.

blocks.text: Inclusive course design principles are covered in [universal design for learning](/glossary/universal-design-for-learning). Industry context for consumer banking is on the [financial services](/industries/financial-services) page. The European Commission notes that its AccessibleEU initiative supports application of EU accessibility law "through training and capacity building", which is a public resource for teams starting from scratch.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry links each accessibility requirement, the role that delivers it, and the standard version it was taught against. When a harmonized standard or national rule changes, the affected modules and learners can be identified from the requirement rather than found by search.

faqs.q: Is staff training under the European Accessibility Act mandatory?
faqs.a: Not as a standalone article. Recital 20 says service providers should ensure proper and continuous training, and Article 13(3) requires procedures that keep services conforming. Whether training is a legal duty in a given country depends on the national transposing law, so check it in each Member State where the service is provided.

faqs.q: Does the Act apply to internal staff training platforms?
faqs.a: The Act covers listed services provided to consumers, not internal tools as such. A learning platform used only by employees is not one of the Article 2(2) services. Employers may still have accessibility duties under employment and equality law, and customer-facing training delivered through a covered service, such as banking or e-commerce, falls within that service's requirements.

faqs.q: What does continuous training mean in practice?
faqs.a: The Directive does not define a frequency. A defensible approach is training at onboarding, refreshers at a fixed interval, and retraining when the service, the accessibility requirements, or the declared standard changes. Those change triggers mirror Article 13(3), which already requires providers to take such changes into account.

Microenterprises providing services are exempt from the Annex I service requirements under Article 4(5). A microenterprise employs fewer than 10 persons and has annual turnover or balance sheet total of EUR 2 million or less. The exemption does not cover larger small and medium-sized enterprises, which must comply.
